title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether generative AI assistance changes students’ writing self-efficacy, and whether the effects depend on where AI intervenes in the writing process. The paper is motivated by concerns that AI can both support writing and potentially reduce learner agency, ownership, and confidence if overused or used at the wrong stage.

The intervention compared four conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment: no AI, ideation-stage AI only, sentence-level AI only, and full-process AI. ChatGPT was used as the AI tool, and the study focused on argumentative writing tasks completed by Korean undergraduates. Participants completed two writing cycles in an online session, with self-efficacy measured after each task using a continuous 0–100 scale.

The findings suggest that generative AI does not uniformly improve writing self-efficacy. Full-process AI produced high but mostly stable self-efficacy, though participants reported reduced ownership; sentence-level AI was associated with declines in self-efficacy over time; and ideation-only AI showed the most promising pattern, combining high self-efficacy with positive change across tasks. The authors conclude that the locus of AI support matters more than the amount of support, and that ideation-focused assistance may better preserve agency while supporting confidence.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot for text generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the generative AI writing assistant in four experimental conditions for Korean undergraduates' argumentative writing: sentence-level revision, ideation-only support, full-process support, and a no-AI control condition.

findings.finding_summary: In this pilot experiment with 13 Korean undergraduates, writing self-efficacy differed by AI configuration rather than simply by AI presence. Full AI showed the highest average self-efficacy (M=82.2) but also signs of reduced ownership; Ideation AI showed high self-efficacy (M=80.1) and the steepest increase over time (94M=+11.1); Sentence AI was associated with universal decline in self-efficacy (5/5 participants, 94M=-5.7); No AI was lowest overall (M=61.8). Pairwise effects included Full AI vs No AI g=1.23 (95% CI [-0.60, 3.07]) and Full AI vs Sentence AI g=0.73.
findings.measure: Writing self-efficacy (0-100 scale) across two argumentative writing tasks
findings.confidence_interval: [−0.60, 3.07] for Full AI vs No AI; other CIs not reported

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot experiment with n=13 and non-definitive confidence intervals, so the evidence is preliminary. It is empirical and structured, but the sample is too small for high-confidence causal claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect sizes are large in some comparisons (e.g., g=1.23) and the paper identifies meaningful differences across AI configurations. However, the practical significance is limited by the pilot nature and unstable estimates.
